column5: Craig argues that unity needs one brain in charge: a manager who hands design to others produces patchwork, and seven masters instead of one. Presented as his position; the claim that unity cannot come from a team is contested.

column4: ch-005 and ch-006 actor's body as material
column5: Craig argues the actor's body is useless as artistic material because emotion takes over and the body escapes the mind's control. This directly challenges the actor-direction lineage the course rests on (Stanislavski). Show both sides in the module.

Craig reports that the Moscow Art Theatre gave hundreds of rehearsals to a play and changed scenes until they balanced. Usable as an example of long rehearsal, though he is also critical of their realism.

Craig argues that Shakespeare wrote almost no scene or action directions, so the stage director should interpret from the words alone. Editors added later directions. Check against the text before using.

column4: ch-004 designing from the whole play
column5: Craig's method: think of scene, movement and words together, then choose colour and form from the play's impression. He calls it personal and not for a school, so label it as one designer's method, not a rule.

column4: ch-019 Hamlet production and its limits
column5: In a later note Craig says he produced Hamlet in Moscow, knowing it was impossible, and that the crowd loves a confusion of principles. A candid example of a stated limit, useful as a counterpoint to his manifesto.
